title: From assembly back to C
description:
GCC compiled four C functions with `-O1` into the assembly below. Work out what each one does and write it in C in `solution.c`, with these declarations:

```c
int mystery1(int a, int b);
long mystery2(int n);
int mystery3(const char *s);
int mystery4(int a, int b);
```

Reminders: arguments arrive in `rdi`, `rsi` (their low halves `edi`, `esi`), the result goes in `rax` / `eax`. `lea eax, [rdi+rdi*2]` just computes the address expression `rdi + rdi * 2` into `eax`. `BYTE PTR [rdi]` is the byte at address `rdi`. `cmovg` copies only if the last comparison said "greater"; `sete al` sets `al` to 1 if it said "equal", else 0.

```nasm
mystery1:
        lea     eax, [rdi+rdi*2]
        add     eax, esi
        ret

mystery2:
        cmp     edi, 1
        jle     .L4
        lea     ecx, [rdi+1]
        mov     eax, 2
        mov     edx, 1
.L3:
        imul    rdx, rax
        add     rax, 1
        cmp     rax, rcx
        jne     .L3
.L1:
        mov     rax, rdx
        ret
.L4:
        mov     edx, 1
        jmp     .L1

mystery3:
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rdi]
        test    al, al
        je      .L12
        mov     edx, 0
.L11:
        cmp     al, 32
        sete    al
        movzx   eax, al
        add     edx, eax
        add     rdi, 1
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rdi]
        test    al, al
        jne     .L11
.L8:
        mov     eax, edx
        ret
.L12:
        mov     edx, 0
        jmp     .L8

mystery4:
        mov     edx, edi
        sub     edx, esi
        mov     eax, esi
        sub     eax, edi
        cmp     edi, esi
        cmovg   eax, edx
        ret
```
hints: In `mystery2`, `rax` counts up from 2 and stops when it reaches `n + 1`, and `rdx` starts at 1 and is multiplied by `rax` each round. In `mystery3`, 32 is the character code of a space.
